name: Yara Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at eight at Meridian Medical Supply, which sells gloves, dressings, syringes and the like to hospitals, clinics and pharmacies. I'm the senior buyer for consumables, so I spend the morning with Priya (our analyst) looking at stock and what's coming off contract. Then supplier calls, mostly about delays. The part I like is rescuing a shortage: finding another source the day before a ward runs out. The part that wears me down is that every contract is a fight between cost and reliability, and the cost people always speak louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can all stop hearing about the robot apocalypse. At work I'd tell Priya to keep trying the forecasting add-on we already have, because it does save an hour on a Monday. Online I'd say nothing, because I'm tired of the debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is secure and I get to keep doing the part I'm good at. I do use the forecasting tool now and then and it's fine for routine reorders, but it's wrong about ten percent of the time. That's why they need people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and use the tool a little more for the dull reorders. Perhaps I'd move 300 a month from the current account into the kids' savings. Mostly I'd spend the saved hours on supplier visits, which actually prevent shortages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. Slightly bored, if I'm being truthful, but boredom is a luxury. I'm not carrying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cost people speak louder at Meridian. Who are they?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hollis (our head of procurement) and the finance director, mainly. Our owners are an investment firm who want the margin up every quarter, so every contract gets squeezed. I get why, but it makes my work harder, because a cheap glove that tears is not a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the spare time those small savings give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Supplier visits, mostly. I'd drive out to the factory and look at the line myself, which a spreadsheet will never tell you. A cheap supplier that doesn't pack properly costs us more than it saves, and I'd rather prove that with photos.

say: I'd say the **robot apocalypse** talk was overdone, and the forecasting tool is fine for dull reorders.
I'd tell Priya to keep using the tool for **routine** reorders.
think: The tool is wrong about **ten percent** of the time, and that's why they need me.
My job is secure, though our **owners** keep squeezing every contract.
do: Use the forecasting tool a little more for **dull reorders**.
Move **300 a month** into the children's savings and spend saved hours on supplier visits.
feel: **Fine**, a bit bored, with nothing new to carry.
S0.quote: A cheap glove that tears is not a saving.
fieldNote: Yara's **steady** approach shows up as using a tool she's already proven, not chasing a new one.
Her pressure is the **owners'** margin demands, which is a real worry even without AI change.

steps.text: Use the forecasting tool for routine reorders
Move 300 a month into the children's savings
Visit two supplier factories a quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should pick what to hand over and what to keep, before someone picks for us. To friends I'd say it's real, and it will hit office jobs first. Online I'd say that people who lose out should get retraining paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my own job changes but isn't gone. Comparing quotes, spotting low stock, writing the routine emails: all that goes to software. What stays is judgement, supplier relationships and knowing which delay is a real one. But the team will shrink, and I won't be sure I'm exempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools properly this time, not just now and then. I'd offer to run the pilot at Meridian, so I shape how it's used. I'd also get a course on supply risk, because that's the part software won't own. And I'd get Priya into the pilot with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mixed. It's exciting to be early, and it's worrying that three of the six people in procurement might not be replaced when they leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The quote comparison and the first-draft emails would go first. That's perhaps a third of my week. Then reorder planning. What I'd keep is the call where a supplier tells you something is wrong, and the decision whether to believe them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Meridian to do for Priya, since she's junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a written plan: Priya moves toward supplier risk and data checking, not out the door. I'd argue that Meridian should train Priya, because someone has to check the machine's work. I'd say that to Hollis straight.

say: We should choose what to **hand over** before someone chooses for us.
People who lose out should get **retraining** paid for.
think: My job **changes** rather than goes: judgement and supplier relationships stay, routine comparing goes.
The team will **shrink**, and I can't be sure I'm exempt.
do: Offer to run the **pilot** at Meridian so I shape how tools are used.
Take a course in **supply risk** and bring Priya into the pilot.
feel: **Uneasy** but a bit excited to be early.
S1.quote: I'd argue that Meridian should train Priya, because someone has to check the machine's work.
fieldNote: Yara moves from tool-user to **pilot** owner, a classic steady-adopter step once the change looks proven.
She protects her junior colleague **Priya**, which shows how she thinks about team responsibility.

steps.text: Offer to run the buying-tool pilot at Meridian
Take a supply risk course in the evenings
Bring Priya into the pilot team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to talk about people, not just cost, right now. To friends I'd say governments haven't prepared, and we should be loud. Online I'd say fund retraining and income support from the companies that gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Everything I do at my desk could be done by something cheaper in two years, and I'm not naive about Meridian's owners. They'd cut procurement to a handful of people overnight if the numbers said so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras at once: the second car upgrade, the weekend trips. I'd move into the safe account everything we can. I'd also start building a business case for a new role, supplier assurance, where a human visits sites and signs off. And I'd join the procurement association's push for retraining funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with moments of fear. Two years is so short that I'd be making decisions before I've understood the situation. But I'm not frozen. I'd keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your partner Tomas is a nurse. How does his work change the way you see two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas works the wards, so his job is protected longer. The robots come about three years after the thinking AI, so his work lasts longer, and we'd lean on that. My pay would go first and Tomas's nursing job would last longer, so I feel relief and guilt at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children, Ana and Luka, that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana and Luka that we have savings and a plan, and that Mum and Dad are talking about it every night. I'd say we might have to skip the summer trip. I'd mean it, and I'd also say it will be okay, and hope that's true.

say: We need to talk about **people**, not just cost, and fund retraining from those who gain.
Governments haven't **prepared**, so we should be loud.
think: Everything I do at my desk could be done **cheaper** in two years.
Tomas's hands-on nursing job lasts **longer**, which brings relief and guilt.
do: Cut the extras and move everything possible into the **safe account**.
Pitch a **supplier assurance** role where a human visits sites and signs off.
feel: **Anxious**, with moments of fear, but not frozen.
S2.quote: My pay would go first and Tomas's nursing job would last longer, so I feel relief and guilt at once.
fieldNote: Yara's household has a **hands-on** earner in Tomas, which shapes her mood without making it calm.
Her response is **practical**: a new role pitch and a funding campaign, rather than panic.

steps.text: Move everything spare into the safe account
Cut weekend trips and the second car upgrade
Pitch a supplier assurance role to Hollis
Join the procurement association's retraining campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a real window, and we should use it. To friends I'd say let's not panic yet. Online I'd say fund retraining now, while people can still use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the clock but not the cliff. I think I'd survive the first wave by moving into a role that checks and audits what the machines buy. I'm not sure it lasts to the end, but five years is long enough to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study. A part-time course in supply chain risk, then a certificate in data checking. I'd keep using AI at work and get good at it, so I'm the person who manages it. And I'd save hard, maybe a thousand a month, because the later years could be lean.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Manageable. It feels like planning a long trip, not running from a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you use the five years for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be firefighting. With five I'd be rebuilding, and I could take the course properly and have a new role before the cliff. It also lets Tomas and me plan our money, rather than guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between this and the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably become the person who audits the buying system: someone who can say why it chose a supplier and whether to trust it. If that role exists, I'd have it. If not, I'd rather know early, so I'd start talking to other firms by year two.

say: Five years is a **real window**, so let's use it, not panic.
We should fund **retraining** now, while people can still use it.
think: I'd feel the **clock** but not the cliff.
I might survive the first wave by moving into **auditing** what machines buy.
do: Study **supply chain risk** part-time, then data checking.
Save **a thousand a month** and keep using AI at work.
feel: **Manageable**, like planning a long trip, not running from a fire.
S3.quote: I'd probably become the person who audits the buying system: someone who can say why it chose a supplier and whether to trust it.
fieldNote: Yara's **steady** adaptability becomes a plan: auditor of the machine's buying decisions.
Five years lets her use **savings** as a tool rather than a panic reserve.

steps.text: Take a part-time supply chain risk course
Get good at the buying tools at work
Save a thousand a month for the lean years
Talk to two other firms by year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's coming, so let's plan sensibly and stop arguing about if. To friends I'd say tell your kids to learn things with people in them. Online I'd say whoever makes the gains should fund the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53 by then, so I'd have a good decade to plan and probably a decent pension too. I'm not scared, but I'm not smug. I've seen how fast things move when owners smell savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and use the tools well, because that's an edge. I'd build my pension, and look for a role in supplier assurance or training buyers. And I'd help Ana and Luka think about studies: care, teaching, trades, jobs where people matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little wistful, because I like this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, who in your life would be affected most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas, our household income, and our kids' studies. If Tomas's nursing is safe until the robots come and I move sideways, we'd be okay. It's the kids who'll face a different world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd regret not having used the time. So I'd set checkpoints: certificate in two years, a new role pitch by year four, and no extra debt after that.

say: It's coming, so let's **plan** and stop arguing about if.
I'd tell people to teach their kids things with **people** in them.
think: At 53 I'd have a decade to plan and a decent **pension**, so I'm not scared.
I know how fast owners move when they see **savings**.
do: Keep working, use the tools well, and build the **pension**.
Help my children plan **studies** in care, teaching or trades.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little wistful, because I like this job.
S4.quote: I've seen how fast things move when owners smell savings.
fieldNote: Yara is **calm** here because ten years gives her time, a strong cushion and a partner in hands-on work.
She sets **checkpoints** for herself, which suits her steady, evidence-led style.

steps.text: Build the pension and avoid new debt
Pitch a supplier assurance role by year four
Guide Ana and Luka towards care, teaching or trades
Keep using the buying tools every week

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because pay at the desk goes first and nobody is ready, including my own employer. What would help is paid retraining that actually leads to jobs, some income support for a gap, and companies telling staff early. I'd also want a seat for staff when Meridian decides how to use these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume desk workers like me are fine. We have savings and degrees, but we're still the group that goes first, and I don't think the public knows that.

headlineQuote: We have savings and degrees, but we're still the group that goes first, and I don't think the public knows that.
portrait: Yara is a 43-year-old senior **medical supplies buyer** at Meridian, married to a nurse, with two children and a mortgage.
She is progressive and **steady**: she uses tools once they're proven and pushes for retraining funds and staff voice.
Her mood climbs from calm to **anxious** as AGI speeds up, then eases when she has time to plan.
She plans to become the **auditor** of machine buying and wants her children in people-facing careers.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because desk pay goes first and employers aren't ready.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** that leads to jobs, income support for a gap, and early warnings from employers.
